PRAX.01.note: Stanford's Zen entry discusses mushin as no-mind within a larger philosophical and embodied practice, avoiding the pop-performance caricature.

exercise.prompt: Choose one well-learned physical skill and describe which parts can become automatic, which still require attention, and why mushin is not mere mindlessness.

PRAX.02.note: The paired Stanford entries distinguish the wider existentialist tradition from Camus's self-described philosophy of the absurd and his criticism of existentialist escape routes.

exercise.prompt: Compare Sartrean meaning-making and Camusian revolt in a two-column table, then apply both responses to the same meaningless setback.

PRAX.03.note: Taleb and Douady's paper gives antifragility a mathematical definition through convex response to variability rather than treating it as a vague synonym for resilience.

article.title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility
article.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb and Raphaël Douady — arXiv

exercise.prompt: Draw one concave and one convex response curve and explain why added variability harms the first system but can benefit the second.

PRAX.04.note: Cornell's official guide provides a concrete, evidence-oriented note workflow with capture, cue, summary, recitation, reflection, and review.

exercise.prompt: Take one page of Cornell notes from a lecture or article, add retrieval questions in the cue column, and write a five-sentence summary without looking back.

PRAX.05.note: Stanford presents Stoic logic, physics, and ethics as one system, correcting the modern reduction of Stoicism to emotional suppression.

exercise.prompt: For one current problem, separate what is up to you from what is not, then write one action guided by virtue rather than by outcome control.

PRAX.06.note: The original passage in Chesterton's The Thing is used instead of later paraphrases, preserving his argument about understanding an institution before reforming it.

article.title: The Thing — The Drift from Domesticity

exercise.prompt: Choose one annoying rule or legacy feature, investigate the failure it originally prevented, and propose a replacement that preserves that function.

PRAX.07.note: Stanford's current identity-over-time entry uses Theseus' ship to introduce competing accounts of persistence, constitution, replacement, and reassembly.

exercise.prompt: Apply the Ship of Theseus puzzle to a software system whose modules are gradually rewritten, then define three different criteria for calling it the same system.

PRAX.08.note: Stanford's simplicity entry separates evidential, pragmatic, syntactic, and ontological simplicity and explains why Occam's Razor is not simply 'pick the easiest story.'

exercise.prompt: Compare two explanations by counting assumptions, parameters, predictive consequences, and ad hoc exceptions rather than judging which sounds simpler.

PRAX.09.note: Yale's lecture introduces the classic trolley cases within a broader course on moral psychology, consequentialism, intention, and doing versus allowing harm.

exercise.prompt: Compare switch, footbridge, and loop variants, stating what changes in intention, physical means, personal force, and expected consequences.

PRAX.10.note: Stanford's Daoism entry situates wu wei within early Chinese debates about action, guidance, spontaneity, and non-coercive rule.

exercise.prompt: Identify one task where extra force creates resistance, then redesign the process around timing, environment, and response rather than direct control.

PRAX.11.note: Ericsson and Harwell clarify the original definition of deliberate practice and distinguish structured improvement from accumulated hours or casual repetition.

article.title: Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice on the Acquisition of Expert Performance
article.source: K. Anders Ericsson and Kyle W. Harwell — Frontiers in Psychology

exercise.prompt: Turn one broad skill into a 30-minute practice block with a narrow target, measurable error, immediate feedback, repetition, and reflection.

PRAX.12.note: The resource covers the classical via negativa—speaking by negation about what exceeds concepts—while the exercise carefully adapts subtraction as a practical heuristic.

exercise.prompt: Take one overloaded routine or system and remove one element at a time, recording which removals preserve the goal and which destroy a necessary function.
